extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (epistemology and moral philosophy)
extracted.subtask_description: A conceptual framework for evaluating moral actions (as conforming or disagreeing with rules) and for assessing the clarity/distinctness of ideas; distinguishes standards (divine, civil, opinion) and gives criteria for clear/obscure and distinct/confused ideas with causes and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral relation (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral relation is the conformity or disagreement men’s voluntary actions have to a rule to which they are referred, and by which they are judged of; which ... may be called MORAL RELATION.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral evaluation consists in comparing a voluntary action with a rule and noting agreement or disagreement; this comparison is central to naming actions morally good or bad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral good and evil (measure)
rubrics_metrics.description: MORAL GOOD AND EVIL ... is only THE CONFORMITY OR DISAGREEMENT OF OUR VOLUNTARY ACTIONS TO SOME LAW, WHEREBY GOOD OR EVIL IS DRAWN ON US, FROM THE WILL AND POWER OF THE LAW-MAKER; which good and evil, pleasure or pain, attending our observance or breach of the law by the decree of the law-maker, is that we call REWARD and PUNISHMENT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging moral good/evil, treat pleasure/pain (and rewards/punishments imposed by a law-maker) as the operative consequences; distinguish moral consequences from natural consequences of actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of enforcement for a law
rubrics_metrics.description: Since it would be utterly in vain to suppose a rule set to the free actions of men, without annexing to it some enforcement of good and evil to determine his will, we must, wherever we suppose a law, suppose also some reward or punishment annexed to that law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A putative moral or legal rule should be considered unsuccessful as a governing law unless it carries enforceable rewards or punishments (beyond the natural consequences of the act) to motivate compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three sorts of law as measures
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws that men generally refer their actions to, to judge of their rectitude or obliquity, seem to me to be these three:—1. The DIVINE law. 2. The CIVIL law. 3. The law of OPINION or REPUTATION.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating actions, explicitly state which of these three standards you are using (sin/duty by divine law; criminal/innocent by civil law; virtue/vice by opinion/reputation) to avoid category confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divine law as ultimate touchstone
rubrics_metrics.description: That God has given a rule whereby men should govern themselves ... This is the only true touchstone of moral rectitude; and, by comparing them to this law, it is that men judge of the most considerable moral good or evil of their actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one adopts divine law as the standard, moral evaluation treats God's promulgated rule and its infinite rewards/punishments as decisive for duties and sins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil law as measure of crime and innocence
rubrics_metrics.description: The CIVIL LAW—the rule set by the commonwealth to the actions of those who belong to it—is another rule to which men refer their actions; to judge whether they be criminal or no ... the force of the Commonwealth, engaged to protect the lives, liberties, and possessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the enacted laws and their institutional enforcement to determine criminality or innocence; consider the state's power and its specific punishments when applying this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of opinion/reputation as measure of virtue and vice
rubrics_metrics.description: The LAW OF OPINION OR REPUTATION ... Virtue and vice ... are constantly attributed only to such actions as in each country and society are in reputation or discredit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess virtue/vice by public approbation or blame within a given society; recognize that reputation and fashion function as enforcement mechanisms (commendation/discredit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue corresponds to public praise
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue is every where, that which is thought praiseworthy; and nothing else but that which has the allowance of public esteem is called virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming an action is virtuous, justify that claim by showing it is generally approved or praised in the relevant social context; be wary of cross-societal variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social enforcement (commendation and discredit)
rubrics_metrics.description: The penalties that attend the breach of God’s laws some, nay perhaps most men, seldom seriously reflect on: ... But no man escapes the punishment of their censure and dislike, who offends against the fashion and opinion of the company he keeps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize social censure and praise as powerful motivators; when predicting compliance or behavior, weigh social sanctions heavily alongside legal or religious penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morality as relation vs positive description
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral actions may be regarded either absolutely, or as ideas of relation. ... in this sense they are as much POSITIVE ABSOLUTE ideas ... Secondly, our actions are considered as good, bad, or indifferent; and in this respect they are RELATIVE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate actions both (a) as positive mixed modes (what the action is in itself) and (b) in relation to the relevant rule; both perspectives are necessary for full moral appraisal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding denomination-based moral error
rubrics_metrics.description: Because very frequently the positive idea of the action, and its moral relation, are comprehended together under one name ... the relation itself is less taken notice of; and there is often no distinction made between the positive idea of the action, and the reference it has to a rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let a name (e.g., 'stealing') automatically determine moral judgment; examine the action's circumstances and the rule applied (example: taking a sword from a madman is 'stealing' in name but may not be sinful).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations terminate in simple ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: All relation terminates in, and is ultimately founded on, those simple ideas we have got from sensation or reflection ... all we have in our thoughts ... is nothing but some simple ideas, or collections of simple ideas, compared one with another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For precise moral or conceptual analysis, decompose relations into their constituent simple ideas derived from sensation or reflection; use this decomposition to make comparisons explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear vs obscure ideas (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Our simple ideas are CLEAR, when they are such as the objects themselves from whence they were taken did or might, in a well-ordered sensation or perception, present them. ... they are obscure so far as they either want anything of the original exactness, or have lost any of their first freshness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge an idea as clear if it corresponds to a proper sensory/reflection-derived impression and can be readily produced by the mind; label ideas obscure when impressions were weak or memory faded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct vs confused ideas (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A DISTINCT idea is that wherein the mind perceives a difference from all other; and a CONFUSED idea is such an one as is not sufficiently distinguishable from another, from which it ought to be different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An idea is distinct when its boundaries vis-à-vis other ideas are perceived; call an idea confused when it fails to be sufficiently separable from related ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of confused ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The defaults which usually occasion this confusion, I think, are, First, complex ideas made up of too few simple ones. Secondly, their simple ones jumbled disorderly together. Thirdly, their simple ones mutable and undetermined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To diagnose confusion, check (a) whether the complex idea omits differentiating simples, (b) whether components are disordered so membership is unclear, and (c) whether the idea's components vary across uses; these defects make the application of names uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusion arises from names and reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas, as ranked under names, ... are the occasion of denominating ideas distinct or confused ... That which makes it confused is, when it is such that it may as well be called by another name as that which it is expressed by.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to how names (words) carry tacit references and can create confusion; ensure that names are applied steadily to a determinate combination of simple ideas to avoid semantic confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examining confusion by identifying the confounded pair
rubrics_metrics.description: Confusion making it a difficulty to separate two things that should be separated, concerns always two ideas; Whenever, therefore, we suspect any idea to be confused, we must examine what other it is in danger to be confounded with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you detect confusion, explicitly identify the alternative idea(s) it is being mistaken for; this comparative diagnosis helps restore distinctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy: precise collection and steady naming
rubrics_metrics.description: The way to prevent it is to collect and unite into one complex idea, as precisely as is possible, all those ingredients whereby it is differenced from others; and to them, so united in a determinate number and order, apply steadily the same name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To remove confusion, define complex ideas by listing their specific simple-idea ingredients in determinate order and consistently use one name for that precise combination; this is the recommended corrective practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex ideas can be partly distinct and partly confused
rubrics_metrics.description: Our complex ideas, being made up of collections, and so variety of simple ones, may accordingly be very clear and distinct in one part, and very obscure and confused in another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a complex concept, assess each constituent part separately; accept mixed evaluations (some components distinct, others confused) rather than forcing a single label.
